problem.statement: Standard .NET multicast delegate events store subscribers in a list, so unsubscribing (-=) is O(n); at large subscriber counts (hundreds of thousands to millions) this makes dispose-time unsubscription a severe CPU/latency bottleneck.

persona.primary: WPF/.NET developer with large dynamic subscriber counts on shared events

context.situation: A .NET/WPF app has a shared value that up to millions of dynamically created components subscribe to and unsubscribe from (on dispose) via standard events, and stress testing reveals unsubscribe alone consumes >90% CPU for seconds at a time.

current_workarounds: Considering switching to weak event handlers so components don't need to explicitly unsubscribe at all
existing_substitutes: WeakEventManager / weak event pattern (considered, not confirmed adopted)

possible_wedges.offer: Roslyn/VS analyzer that flags event subscribe/unsubscribe patterns likely to hit O(n) scaling at high subscriber counts and suggests scalable alternatives (weak events, indexed dispatch)
Static scan of a legacy .NET/WPF codebase for large-fan-out event usage patterns as part of an audit report

risks: Single evidence item (n=1); no confirmation this is a widespread pattern beyond one Stack Overflow question
No explicit willingness to pay or mention of budget/tooling spend
Not clear the poster's scenario (millions of subscribers) is common in typical WPF/.NET audit targets vs. an edge case
No mention of OwnAudit or audit tooling specifically in the evidence -- link to the audit-tool wedge is an inference, not stated
Workaround (weak events) is only proposed/considered, not validated as adopted or effective

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: .NET/WPF developers who hit O(n) event-unsubscribe slowdowns at large subscriber counts would engage with (and want a tool to catch) this anti-pattern before it becomes a stress-test crisis.
cheapest_experiment.input: A short technical post/analyzer-rule writeup describing the 'event unsubscribe is O(n) over subscriber list' anti-pattern, shared on r/dotnet, Stack Overflow, and .NET blogs, linking to a one-page signup/waitlist describing an audit-tool check for it.
cheapest_experiment.output: Number of waitlist signups or reply comments describing their own large-subscriber-count event performance pain.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: A developer submits their email to the waitlist or replies describing a matching real-world incident.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Fewer than 5 relevant signups/replies after 2 weeks despite 1000+ views
